ad13_black.topic: Black Americans: mobility, wealth, Social Security exclusions, homeownership, education, health

claims.text: Chetty et al. (20 million children): Black and American Indian children have substantially lower upward mobility than other groups; Black children of bottom-quintile parents have a 2.5% chance of reaching the top quintile vs 10.6% for whites

Chetty et al.: Black children raised in top-quintile families are almost as likely to fall to the bottom quintile as to stay at the top; white children are nearly five times as likely to stay as to fall

Chetty et al.: Black women earn slightly more than white women with the same parent income while Black men earn substantially less; 21% of Black men born to the lowest-income families are incarcerated on a given day; fewer than 5% of Black children grow up in areas with poverty below 10% and more than half of Black fathers present, vs 63% of white children; parental marriage, education, wealth and ability explain very little of the gap; gaps persist on the same block

Chetty et al.: Hispanic upward mobility slightly below whites and Hispanics on a path to move up substantially; Asian immigrants' children have much higher upward mobility than all other groups; Asian children of US-born parents similar to whites; without change Black and American Indian positions unlikely to change

DeWitt (SSA, 2010): 1930 Census - about 65% of gainfully employed Black workers (3,564,044 of 5,503,535) were in agriculture or domestic service; the two sectors held 15.5m of 48.8m workers (about 32%); of excluded workers 74% white, 23% Black; 27% of white workers excluded

DeWitt: exclusion proposed by Treasury Secretary Morgenthau in testimony to House Ways and Means, 5 February 1935, on grounds the Bureau of Internal Revenue doubted it could collect the taxes; CES staff had also recommended it; 1950 amendments covered regularly employed farm and domestic workers, 1954 amendments the rest; DeWitt concludes racial-bias allegations 'do not hold up under detailed scrutiny'

DeWitt names the racial-motive thesis's proponents: Robert Lieberman (OAI 'founded on racial exclusion'), Linda Gordon ('deliberate and mainly racially motivated'), and Alston and Ferrie (class- and race-based paternalism)
NYRB 2023: David Kaiser cited DeWitt against the claim that Southern chairmen forced the exclusions; Adam Hochschild replied that he found DeWitt convincing

Derenoncourt, Kim, Kuhn, Schularick (QJE 2024): white-to-Black per capita wealth ratio about 6 to 1; even with equal wealth-building conditions since Emancipation convergence would be distant; convergence stalled after 1950 and the gap has widened since the 1980s as capital gains mainly benefited white households and income convergence stopped

Barsky, Bound, Charles, Lupton (2001/2002): differences in earnings account for roughly two-thirds of the overall Black-white wealth gap using a nonparametric reweighting method; standard Blinder-Oaxaca gives substantially different estimates

Darity, Hamilton et al. (2018) via Fortune: Black households headed by a college graduate hold less wealth than white households headed by someone without a high school diploma; white households with an employed head have more than 10 times the wealth of similar Black households; authors propose baby bonds
Census CPS 2024: 29.6% of Black adults 25+ held a bachelor's degree (8.675m) vs 38.6% of white adults
NCHS life tables 2024: life expectancy at birth total 79.0; Hispanic 81.8; non-Hispanic AIAN 71.1; non-Hispanic Asian 85.8; non-Hispanic Black 74.8; non-Hispanic white 78.9

ad13_immig.topic: Immigrants and Latino Americans: taxes paid, benefit exclusions, fiscal effects, 2025-26 law

claims.text: ITEP: undocumented immigrants paid $96.7bn in federal, state and local taxes in 2022: $59.4bn federal, $37.3bn state and local (nearly 39%)
ITEP: of the federal total, $25.7bn Social Security, $6.4bn Medicare and $1.8bn unemployment insurance taxes, funding programmes these workers are barred from

ITEP: in 40 states undocumented immigrants pay higher state and local tax rates than the top 1% there; more than a third of their taxes are payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare they cannot access; they often cannot claim the CTC and EITC; work authorisation would raise payments by $40.2bn to $136.9bn

NASEM 2016: first-generation immigrants are more costly to governments, mainly at state and local level, than the native-born; the second generation are among the strongest fiscal contributors, contributing the most of any generation to state balance sheets; wage effects, where found, fall on native-born high-school dropouts and prior immigrants

OBBBA (signed 4 July 2025) per USCCB summary: 1% excise tax on cash/money-order remittances from 1 January 2026 (bank account and card transfers exempt); CTC requires the filer or one spouse to have an SSN; SNAP eligibility ended for refugees, asylees and others; Medicaid/CHIP limited to green-card holders, Cuban/Haitian entrants and COFA migrants from 1 October 2026; ACA premium credits limited from 1 January 2027; Medicare limited similarly

PNPI: Latino adults 25+ with a bachelor's degree 20.8% in 2023, up from 14.0% in 2013 (national 36.2%); 32.8% of Latinos 18-24 enrolled in college in 2022 vs 39.0% overall; Latino enrolment 2.98m (fall 2012) to 3.78m

ad13_asian_native.topic: Asian Americans (inequality, subgroups, model minority) and Native Americans (Dawes, Cobell, trust-land lending, poverty, health)

claims.text: Pew 2018: 90/10 income ratio among Asians 10.7 in 2016, up 77% since 1970 (implying about 6.0); Blacks 9.8, whites 7.8, Hispanics 7.8; Asians at 90th percentile earned 13% more than whites, at the 10th percentile 17% less (8% more in 1970); median annual income 2016 Asians $51,288, whites $47,958, Blacks $31,082, Hispanics $30,400

Pew 2018: immigrants accounted for 81% of Asian adult population growth 1970-2016 after the 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act; bachelor's attainment ranged from 9% (Bhutanese) to 72% (Indians); median household income from $36,000 (Burmese) to $100,000 (Indians)
Pew (2022 ACS) via NPR: about 1 in 10 Asian Americans in poverty; Burmese 19%, Hmong about 17%, Mongolian about 16%; Indian about 6%; Filipino, Japanese, Nepalese, Sri Lankan 6-9%

William Petersen, 'Success Story, Japanese-American Style', NYT Magazine 9 January 1966, among articles that introduced the 'model minority' concept; credited cultural values and contrasted Japanese Americans with African Americans; scholars argue the concept was used to criticise social programmes

Dawes Act (1887): heads of families allotted 160 acres, others up to 80, title held in trust 25 years; 'surplus' land sold to non-Indians; Indian-held land fell from 138 million to 48 million acres by 1934 when allotment stopped; almost half of the remainder arid or semiarid

Cobell settlement $3.4bn: $1.5bn for accounting and trust mismanagement claims, $1.9bn land consolidation fund buying fractionated interests (up to $60m scholarships); nearly 500,000 class members; Claims Resolution Act passed 30 Nov 2010, signed 8 Dec 2010; court approval 4 Aug 2011; final 24 Nov 2012; over 2.9m fractional interests owned by about 220,000 individuals

HAC: reservation trust land cannot be sold or used as mortgage collateral; borrowers hold leaseholds; BIA review; reservation poverty 29.2% vs 15.5% nationally; 2015 HMDA loans 22.3 per 1,000 US residents vs 1.9 per 1,000 reservation residents; on-reservation Native denial rate 46% vs 29%; manufactured homes 39% of on-reservation applications vs 7%; Section 184 (1992) guarantees, >90% of loans off-reservation, fewer than 200 reservation loans a year 2005-2016

Minneapolis Fed 2018: AIAN manufactured-home loan denial rate about 75% in mostly on-reservation tracts (2015-16) vs about 25% for site-built; manufactured-home share of AIAN applications about 30% off-reservation vs over 75% on-reservation; chattel loan APR about 1.5 points above mortgages (CFPB); trust status may partly explain, not concluded
USAFacts (Census, 2024): poverty rate American Indian and Alaska Native 19.3%, highest of groups listed; Asian 7.5%
Census 2025: 7.7m AIAN alone or in combination (2024); 574 federally recognised tribes; 325 federally recognised reservations
